title: Hüzün, keyif and kolay gelsin
goal: Judge the style of a text, keep it in translation, and handle words that have no English twin.

intro.text: Style lives in sentence length, word origin, register and rhythm, and a translation in the wrong register is a mistranslation. For *hüzün*, *gurbet*, *keyif* or *Kolay gelsin*, which have no English twin, keep and explain, say what an English speaker would say, or say nothing.

vocab.en: I'm not in the mood; I'm feeling low
the evil eye (nazar değmek: to be struck by the evil eye)
Turkish emigrant worker, especially in Western Europe
faithful (aslına sadık: faithful to the original)

exercises.title: Bir çevirmenin notları
exercises.passage:
Çevirmenler en çok küçük kelimelerden korkar. Geçen ay bir İstanbul romanını İngilizceye çevirirken iki gün “hüzün” kelimesine takıldım. İngilizcede “sadness” var, “melancholy” var; ama ikisi de tam oturmuyor. Romandaki hüzün kişisel bir acı değil; şehrin bütün sokaklarına sinmiş, neredeyse tatlı bir duygu. Sonunda kelimeyi olduğu gibi bıraktım ve ilk geçtiği yere kısa bir dipnot ekledim.

Kahramanın her sabah bakkala “Kolay gelsin!” demesi de ayrı bir sorundu. Kelimesi kelimesine çevirsem okur gülerdi; açıklasam diyalog ağırlaşırdı. Bir İngiliz bakkala sabahları ne denirse onu yazdım: “Morning!”

Editörüm metni okuyunca tek bir şey sordu: “Bu kadar uzun cümleleri neden böldün?” Çünkü Türkçede güzel akan bir cümle, İngilizcede okuru yorabilir. Bana göre çevirmenin işi, kelimeleri değil, okurun yaşayacağı deneyimi taşımaktır.

glossary.en: to become heavy, to slow down

exercises.translation: Translators fear small words most. Last month, while translating an Istanbul novel into English, I got stuck for two days on the word hüzün. English has sadness, and melancholy, but neither quite fits. The hüzün of the novel is not a personal grief; it is a feeling that has soaked into every street of the city, almost a sweet one. In the end I left the word as it was and added a short footnote where it first appears. The hero's 'Kolay gelsin!' to the grocer every morning was another problem. If I translated it word for word, readers would laugh; if I explained it, the dialogue would drag. I wrote what you would say to an English grocer in the morning: 'Morning!' When my editor read the text, she asked one thing: 'Why did you split such long sentences?' Because a sentence that flows beautifully in Turkish can tire the reader in English. In my view, a translator's job is to carry not the words but the experience the reader will have.

questions.q: What did the translator finally do with *hüzün*?
options: Kept the word and explained it in a footnote
Translated it as sadness every time
questions.explain: *Kelimeyi olduğu gibi bıraktım ve ilk geçtiği yere kısa bir dipnot ekledim.*

questions.q: Why did she write **Morning!** for *Kolay gelsin*?
options: It is what an English speaker would say to a shopkeeper
questions.explain: A functional equivalent: the greeting that fits the same moment.

questions.q: Which statement fits the last paragraph?
options: A translator carries the reader's experience, not the words
Long sentences must never be split
English sentences are always shorter than Turkish ones

questions.q: How would you describe the style of the text itself?
options: Personal and plain: first person, everyday words, short sentences
Ottoman: Arabic and Persian words and the izafet
questions.explain: *Takıldım*, *bıraktım*, *yazdım*: a personal voice; the longest sentence has three verbs.

exercises.question: Which version of the same news is written in official style?

why.1: Everyday: news passed on with `-mIş`, and *haberin olsun*.
why.2: Literary: the verb first, then a short sentence for effect.
why.3: News style: short and passive, but without the official verbal noun and `-mIştIr`.

exercises.explain: A passive (*karar verilmiş*), a verbal noun (*ertelenmesine*) and `-DIr`: the marks of official Turkish. English: **It has been decided to postpone the meeting.**

accept: I'm not in the mood at all this evening.
I am not in the mood [this evening|tonight]
I am not in the mood at all tonight
I really am not in the mood (at all) [this evening|tonight]
I am really not in the mood (at all) [this evening|tonight]
[This evening|Tonight] I [am not|really am not|am really not] in the mood (at all)
I [do not|really do not] feel like it (at all) [this evening|tonight]
I [am not feeling|do not feel] (very) [great|good|well] [this evening|tonight]
I am not feeling up to much [this evening|tonight]
I am [feeling low|feeling down|in a bad mood|out of sorts] [this evening|tonight]
exercises.explain: *Keyfim yok*: no pleasure in me, so **I'm not in the mood**, or **I'm feeling low**. *Keyif* drops its i before a vowel: *keyfim*.

exercises.en: Have you moved into your new home? Congratulations!
exercises.explain: *Hayırlı olsun* is said for anything new: a home, a car, a job. *Kolay gelsin* is for someone at work, *Geçmiş olsun* for illness or bad luck.
*Keyfini çıkarmak* (to enjoy to the full) takes a genitive: *tatilin keyfini*. The formula *İyi tatiller!* says the same thing in two words.

exercises.question: A friend praises your new car and adds *Nazar değmesin!* What is the closest English habit?

why.1: That follows a sneeze; *Çok yaşa!* is its Turkish twin.
why.2: Before an exam, Turkish says *Başarılar!* or *Kolay gelsin!*
why.3: For a new car, that is *Hayırlı olsun!*; *Nazar değmesin* comes after praise.

exercises.explain: *Nazar değmesin* wards off the evil eye after a compliment, as English speakers touch or knock on wood after a hopeful remark.

exercises.task: Translate this notice into English, keeping its official tone.
exercises.source: Sayın ziyaretçilerimiz, onarım çalışmaları nedeniyle müzemizin üst katı 15 Mart'a kadar kapalıdır. Anlayışınız için teşekkür ederiz.
models: Dear visitors, the upper floor of the museum is closed until 15 March for restoration work. Thank you for your understanding.
Please note that, owing to restoration work, the museum's upper floor will remain closed until 15 March. We thank you for your understanding.
checklist: Formal English for formal Turkish: **Dear visitors**, **owing to**, **We thank you for your understanding**
`-DIr` in *kapalıdır* adds no doubt: **is closed** or **will remain closed**
The date as English writes it: **15 March** or **March 15**

accept: Hope the work is going well
Hope your day is going well
May it [be easy|come easy] (for you|to you)
exercises.hint: Say what an English speaker would say to someone at work, or translate it literally.
exercises.explain: There is no English formula for this moment. In dialogue, translators write a greeting that fits (**Hope it's going well**, **Morning!**); a literal **May it come easy** works only with a note.

exercises.en: My brother has been living away from home for years.
